title: Articles of Note: Week of October 26, 2026
author: Jason Moore
summary: This weekly curation from ON Classical Education gathers articles relevant to classical and liberal education, each with a short excerpt. The week's picks include Dissident Teacher on why high-expectations classical charters drift from their mission, Christopher Perrin's interview with Jamie Burns about the renewal of classical Christian education in Britain, and Pamela Paul in the Wall Street Journal on Harvard's Humanities 10, a lecture course drawing 90 students to Jane Austen, Smith and Kant. David Butterfield in The New Criterion reflects on how fragile cultural memory is and how information survived from antiquity. Rick Hess interviews school choice advocate Jeanne Allen, Michael McShane takes up special-needs school choice, and The Week reports on the English push to teach oracy. Newsweek's Ian Stout argues schools should focus on real intelligence in an AI era, with Sweden's reversal on classroom screens as the warning. Other entries cover business as a liberal art in Alabama, Dan Wang on a Phoenix factory, Henry Oliver on Pride and Prejudice, and Susan McWilliams Barndt on Tocqueville.
points: The curation links classical charters, humanities revival at Harvard, and British classical Christian schooling as signs the tradition is gaining ground.
Butterfield's essay reminds readers that a culture's shared store of knowledge is not preserved by any divine right and can be lost.
Several picks converge on oracy and screens: England's push to elevate oracy and Sweden's removal of classroom screens frame a debate about what schools should prioritize.
Dissident Teacher's charter piece identifies how mission drift happens inside public classical schools and links to free tools.
Literary and civic items (Pride and Prejudice, Tocqueville, business as a liberal art) show the breadth of what the curator counts as classical and liberal education.
quotes: Just a few weeks ago, 57 of my students took turns standing up in front of their classmates to recite “Sonnet 44: How do I love thee?” by Elizabeth Barrett Browning.
Those who see the humanities, heavy coursework and value of a Harvard education as gravely imperiled can take heart in the phenomenon that is Humanities 10.

The lights, we must never forget, can always go out. The shared store of information that a culture values is not preserved by any divine right; with just a few wrong turns taken, the entirety of its riches can be lost, not just temporarily but even irrevocably.
It’s odd, then, that you were almost certainly never taught public speaking in the way you were taught geography or maths.
Sweden spent years putting screens in classrooms. Now, they are being taken out.
Then we discover that students who use it to skip the work of thinking do not learn to think.
Tocqueville was just 25 years old, but he was determined to figure out what made the United States tick.
